segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through whom we have also gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we boast in the hope of the glory of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For while we were still weak, Christ died at the right time for the ungodly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person perhaps someone might even dare to die.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Much more, then, having now been justified by his blood, we will be saved through him from the wrath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we will be saved by his life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only that, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all people, because all sinned—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not charged to anyone's account when there is no law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a pattern of the one who was to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the gracious gift is not like the trespass. For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound to the many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the gift is not like what came through the one who sinned. For the judgment following one trespass led to condemnation, but the gracious gift following many trespasses led to justification.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if by the trespass of the one death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, as through one trespass condemnation came to all people, so also through one righteous act justification that brings life came to all people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the law came in alongside so that the trespass might increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness, leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

notes.note: Many early and important manuscripts read 'let us have peace' (a difference of one vowel, which sounded alike when the letter was read aloud). The edition translated here, with most modern editors and translations, reads the statement 'we have peace', which suits the argument: Paul is describing what follows from justification, not urging it.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'justify', 'justification', 'righteous' and 'righteousness' in this chapter all translate forms of the same root. The verb means to declare or set someone in the right, as a court does. Translations from Latin and most other languages use their one word for 'justice' throughout, and some scholars prefer 'justice' in English as well.

The same verb occurs in verses 2, 3 and 11, and its ordinary meaning is to boast or take pride in something. Many English versions soften it to 'rejoice' or 'exult'; others have 'boast'. 'Boast' is kept here because Paul has just excluded boasting in one's own standing (3:27; 4:2) and now names what believers may rightly boast in. The form could also be read as 'let us boast'.

The Greek phrase can mean God's love for us or our love for God. Most interpreters take it as God's love for us, since verses 6–8 go on to describe how God has shown that love. A minority, following Augustine, read it as love for God.

The Greek says simply 'the wrath'. Many translations add 'of God' for clarity, and that is certainly whose wrath is meant: the coming judgment on wrongdoing that Paul has described in 1:18 and 2:5. The text is left as Paul wrote it.

Paul begins a comparison ('just as...') and breaks off without completing it, turning aside in verses 13–17 to explain and qualify it. The comparison is restarted and finished in verse 18 ('so also...'). The dash at the end of the verse marks the break.

The Greek connecting phrase is brief and much debated. Most modern scholars take it as 'because'. The old Latin translation rendered it 'in whom', that is, in Adam, a reading that was influential in Western teaching on original sin but is now generally thought not to fit the Greek. Some scholars propose 'with the result that all sinned'.

The word meant a mould, model or pattern. Many versions keep 'type', which is a technical term of later theology and no longer clear English, while some others also have 'pattern'. Paul's point is that Adam, as one man whose act affected all, corresponds in advance to Christ, though the following verses stress how unlike the two are.

The Greek noun is formed from the word for 'grace' and means something given as an act of favour. 'Free gift' is the usual rendering; 'gracious gift' is used so that the link with 'grace' later in the verse can be heard. Paul uses two other, more ordinary words for 'gift' in verses 15–17, which are rendered simply 'gift'.

'The many' is a Semitic way of speaking of the whole mass of people as contrasted with the one; it does not mean 'many but not all'. The same group is called 'all people' in verses 12 and 18. How far Paul means the second 'all' and 'the many' to extend is debated, since verse 17 speaks of 'those who receive' the gift.

This Greek noun usually means a righteous requirement or a righteous act, and it is rendered 'righteous act' in verse 18. Here it stands as the opposite of 'condemnation', and nearly all interpreters take it to mean the verdict that sets someone in the right. Paul probably chose this form instead of his usual word for justification (used in verse 18) because its ending matches the Greek words for 'judgment' and 'condemnation'.

The Greek can equally be read 'the trespass of one... the righteous act of one', since 'one' may refer to the person and not to the deed. Either way the reference is to Adam's disobedience and to Christ's obedience, usually understood as his death. The sentence has no verb in Greek; 'came' is supplied.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

candidates.reason: Central term across the whole New Testament where translators vary between grace, favour and gift, and where a reader needs to see one consistent English word.
Versions alternate between boast, rejoice, exult and glory, which hides Paul's deliberate reuse of the verb in both negative and positive senses across Romans, Corinthians and Galatians.
Rendered variously as tribulation, suffering, affliction, trouble and distress across the New Testament, and 'tribulation' carries end-times associations that a single decision should settle.
It needs a fixed rendering distinct from ἁμαρτία (sin) and παράβασις (transgression), since Paul uses all three side by side and translations blur them.
It recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians and the Pastorals as free gift, gift or spiritual gift, and the link to χάρις is lost unless one rendering is fixed.
